topic: Effects of spaceflight on the human body
hook: What happens to your body in space

slides.title: You get taller
slides.body: Without gravity your spine stretches out. Astronauts grow up to 3% taller, then shrink back on Earth.
slides.image_prompt: A glowing human spine model floating weightless inside a space station module, Earth visible through a round window

slides.title: Your bones thin out
slides.body: Weight-bearing bones like hips and legs can lose 1% to 1.5% of their mass every month in orbit.
slides.image_prompt: A white bone floating in dark space, slowly crumbling into tiny glowing particles drifting away

slides.title: Puffy face, bird legs
slides.body: Body fluids drift upward, so faces swell and legs slim down. Astronauts really call it 'puffy face, bird legs'.
slides.image_prompt: Water droplets floating upward inside a space capsule, forming wobbly spheres against metal walls

slides.title: Your eyes change shape
slides.body: Fluid pressure can flatten the back of the eye. Some astronauts need stronger glasses after long missions.
slides.image_prompt: A pair of glasses floating weightless in front of a spacecraft window with Earth glowing below

slides.title: Food tastes bland
slides.body: The fluid shift leaves astronauts with stuffy noses, which dulls taste. Many start craving hot sauce.
slides.image_prompt: Sealed space food packets and a small bottle of hot sauce floating weightless inside a space station

cta: Follow so you never miss the next one
caption:
Spend a few months in orbit and your body starts rewriting itself. NASA has measured astronauts coming home up to 3% taller, with thinner bones and changed eyes.

Most of it reverses back on Earth, but some changes stay for months or even years. That is one of the biggest hurdles for a trip to Mars.

Would you still go to space knowing all this?
